h1: New York HOA Election Challenge Demand Letter
metaTitle: New York HOA Election Challenge Demand Letter Tool
metaDescription: Generate a New York HOA election challenge demand letter citing NY law. Contest improper board elections, voting violations, and proxy fraud quickly and effectively.
statuteCitation: N.Y. Not-for-Profit Corporation Law §§ 608, 618, 621; N.Y. Real Property Law § 339-v
deadline: Four months to start an Article 78 proceeding after the determination becomes final and binding (CPLR 217); written demand should be sent promptly after the disputed election
penalty: Court-ordered new election, invalidation of contested vote results, and recovery of legal fees if authorized by governing documents
introParagraph: If you live in a New York condominium or homeowners association and believe the most recent board election was unfair, improperly noticed, or tainted by proxy abuse, state law gives you real leverage. New York's Not-for-Profit Corporation Law and Real Property Law set strict requirements for how HOA and condo elections must be conducted, including notice, quorum, voting procedures, and inspection of records. A well-drafted demand letter citing the specific statutes can pressure the board to recount votes, hold a new election, or release records before you ever step into court. This page explains how New York law treats election challenges and how a formal demand letter can resolve the dispute without expensive litigation.
lawExplanation: Most New York HOAs and condominiums are organized as not-for-profit corporations, meaning they are governed by the New York Not-for-Profit Corporation Law (N-PCL). Section 608 sets the quorum for member meetings (a majority of the votes entitled to be cast unless the certificate or by-laws provide a lesser quorum), while Section 618 lets any member aggrieved by an election petition the Supreme Court, which may confirm the election, order a new election, or take such other action as justice may require. Section 621 gives members of record for at least six months the right to examine the minutes of member proceedings and the list of members on five days' written demand, and, for a homeowners association, to review invoices, ledgers, bank accounts, reconciliations, and contracts related to the expenditure of dues — critical evidence when challenging an election. For condominiums, the Condominium Act (Real Property Law Article 9-B, § 339-v) requires the by-laws to provide for the nomination and election of the board of managers, so the election must follow the by-laws. Cooperative apartments are additionally governed by the Business Corporation Law. Common grounds for an election challenge in New York include: failure to provide proper written notice of the meeting, lack of a quorum, improper handling or solicitation of proxies, denial of access to the membership list before the vote, counting of ineligible ballots, board interference with candidate nominations, and conflicts of interest among inspectors of election. New York courts have repeatedly invalidated HOA and condo elections where boards ignored their own bylaws or the N-PCL's procedural safeguards. Importantly, members do not need to prove the outcome would have changed — material procedural violations alone can be enough to void an election. Before filing in court, sending a detailed demand letter is often the fastest path to a remedy, because boards and their counsel know that a petition under N-PCL § 618 or a proceeding under CPLR Article 78, which can raise whether a determination violated lawful procedure or was arbitrary and capricious (CPLR § 7803), may result in a court-ordered new election.
letterStrategy: A New York HOA election challenge demand letter works because it puts the board on formal notice that a member is prepared to file an N-PCL § 618 petition or an Article 78 proceeding (CPLR Article 78) if the dispute is not resolved. The letter should identify the specific election being challenged, list each procedural violation (improper notice, proxy irregularities, denied records inspection, quorum failures, etc.), and cite the controlling statute and bylaw provisions. Including a preservation-of-evidence demand is critical: ask the board to preserve ballots, proxies, sign-in sheets, and electronic voting data. Boards frequently settle these disputes once they receive a clear, statute-based letter, because litigation exposes them to court costs, potential personal liability for directors who acted in bad faith, and disclosure of internal communications. The letter also creates a paper trail that strengthens any later court filing and may support a fee-shifting claim if the governing documents allow recovery of legal fees by a prevailing member. A well-drafted demand can also trigger directors' and officers' insurance notice obligations, prompting the carrier to push the board toward resolution.
proceduralNotes: If the demand letter does not resolve the dispute, a New York member can file an N-PCL § 618 petition in the Supreme Court of the county where the HOA is located, or an Article 78 proceeding (CPLR § 7803 lists the questions it can raise). A proceeding under CPLR Article 78 generally must be started within four months after the determination becomes final and binding (CPLR § 217). Small claims court (with a $10,000 limit) is generally not appropriate for election challenges because the remedy sought is equitable — a new election or invalidation — rather than money damages. Members should act quickly; delay can be treated as waiver.

faq.q: What are the most common grounds to challenge an HOA election in New York?
faq.a: The strongest grounds include inadequate written notice of the meeting, failure to meet the quorum requirement in N-PCL § 608, improper solicitation or counting of proxies, denial of a member's right to examine the list of members under § 621, board interference with candidate nominations, and inspectors of election with undisclosed conflicts of interest. Violations of the association's own bylaws — even if technical — are also frequently sufficient under New York case law to invalidate an election, regardless of whether the outcome would have changed.

faq.q: How long do I have to challenge an HOA election in New York?
faq.a: If you plan to file an Article 78 proceeding, you generally must start it within four months after the determination you are challenging becomes final and binding on you (CPLR § 217). A petition under N-PCL § 618 should also be filed promptly to avoid laches arguments. Sending a demand letter promptly after the election is strongly recommended, because delay can weaken your claim and may be treated as acceptance of the results. Acting quickly also helps preserve ballots and proxies before they are discarded.

faq.q: Can I see the ballots and proxies after a contested election?
faq.a: Partly. Under N-PCL § 621, a member of record for at least six months may examine the minutes of member proceedings and the list of members on five days' written demand, and members of a homeowners association may review invoices, ledgers, bank accounts, and contracts related to the expenditure of dues. Ballots themselves are not listed in that section, so a court may need to order their production once a § 618 petition or Article 78 proceeding is filed. A demand letter should formally request inspection of all election-related records and ask the board to preserve ballots, proxies, sign-in sheets, and any electronic voting logs pending resolution of the dispute.

faq.q: Do I need a lawyer to send a New York HOA election challenge letter?
faq.a: No. New York members can send their own demand letter, and a clearly written letter citing N-PCL §§ 608, 618, and 621 and the relevant bylaw provisions is often enough to prompt a board response. However, if the matter proceeds to Supreme Court under CPLR Article 78 or N-PCL § 618, hiring an attorney experienced in not-for-profit corporate governance or condominium law is strongly recommended, because procedural rules and pleading standards are strict and missteps can result in dismissal.

faq.q: What remedies can a New York court order if my election challenge succeeds?
faq.a: Under N-PCL § 618, the Supreme Court can confirm the election, order a new election, or take such other action as justice may require. In an Article 78 proceeding, a court can review whether the board's determination was made in violation of lawful procedure, was affected by an error of law, or was arbitrary and capricious (CPLR § 7803). If the governing documents authorize fee-shifting, a prevailing member may also recover attorneys' fees. Monetary damages are generally not awarded in election challenges, since the relief sought is equitable rather than compensatory.
